title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: the Nyaya Sutra sorts every argument into three kinds of talk, and only one of them is looking for the truth

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nyaya, logic: an argument in five parts, said out loud, and the question that does the real work. Where's your pot? Did you find one before you said "because"? A new week begins. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

Three arguments are going on at the same wedding. At one table, two old friends are trying to work out whether a hard decision was right, and each keeps saying, wait, say that again, I think you've got a point. At the next table, two uncles are arguing politics, and neither one is listening; each is just waiting for a gap to land the next blow. And in the corner, somebody has no opinion of his own at all. He just pokes holes in whatever anyone else says. Same noise level. Same raised hands. The Nyaya Sutra would say these are three completely different things, and it gives each one a name.
screen: `THREE ARGUMENTS, ONE WEDDING.` → `SAME NOISE, DIFFERENT AIMS.` → `NYAYA NAMES ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: The first is vada: discussion. In the Nyaya Sutra, vada is talk where both sides use the real means of knowing, perception, inference, and the rest, and set out their reasons in the five parts from yesterday, without contradicting their own starting points. The point of vada is not to win. It's to find out. Later in the Sutra, vada is described as the kind of talk you have with a teacher, a student, or fellow seekers, people who aren't jealous of being right. The second is jalpa: wrangling. Jalpa has all the same parts, but now the aim is victory, and so it reaches for tricks: twisting a word into a meaning the speaker never intended, raising objections that only sound like objections. The third is vitanda: cavil. Vitanda is wrangling with no position of your own. You don't defend anything. You only knock down. So far it sounds like one good kind of talk and two bad ones. But the Sutra adds a turn. It says jalpa and vitanda have a use: they guard a true conclusion the way a hedge of thorny branches guards a sprouting seed. When someone comes only to trample, you may need thorns. So Nyaya doesn't pretend hard argument never happens. It asks you to know which kind you're in, and to remember that the hedge exists for the seed. The seed is the truth, and the garden is vada. Brought down to a kitchen table, that's a practical question. Halfway through any argument, you can ask yourself: am I trying to find out, or am I trying to win?
screen: `VADA: TALK THAT WANTS TO FIND OUT.` · `JALPA: TALK THAT WANTS TO WIN.` · `VITANDA: ONLY KNOCKING DOWN.` · `THORNS THAT GUARD A SEED.` · then, large: `FIND OUT, OR WIN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: replay one argument, gently. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring back a recent disagreement, at home, at work, online. Don't reargue it. Just watch it, as if from the next table. Which of the three was it? Vada, trying to find out? Jalpa, trying to win? Vitanda, only knocking down? Notice which one you were in, and which one you think the other person was in. Then imagine your next sentence in that conversation as vada: one honest question. You don't have to say it. Just find it. If you pray, you can ask for a mind that wants the truth more than the win. The bell holds the time.
Nyaya. Today, its three kinds of talk: vada, discussion that seeks the truth; jalpa, wrangling to win; and vitanda, attacking with no position of your own.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Today, in one disagreement, stop halfway and ask: am I trying to find out, or trying to win? Then ask one real question. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit learning, Nyaya students practice vada, structured discussion with a teacher or fellow students, and formal debate, with each side setting out its reasons step by step, has a place in the tradition.

fork.setup: you're at the wedding. someone comes to your table only to trample on a conclusion you've carefully reached. what does the Nyaya Sutra allow?
options: nothing: only gentle discussion is ever allowed.
wrangling to protect it, like a thorny hedge around a seed.
give up the conclusion to keep the peace.
fork.reveal: the Sutra says jalpa and vitanda can guard a true conclusion the way thorny branches guard a sprouting seed. the hedge is for the seed; the garden is still vada.

original.note: Sanskrit: vada, discussion; in Nyaya, honest talk aimed at the truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: an argument is an argument.
what it means: Nyaya tells apart discussion that wants to find out, wrangling that wants to win, and attacking with no view of your own.
what a scholar hears: Nyaya Sutra 1.2.1–3 defines vada, jalpa and vitanda; 4.2.50 compares jalpa and vitanda to a thorny fence that protects sprouting seeds.

sources.ref: Nyaya Sutra 4.2.47–50 (discussion with the learned; jalpa and vitanda as a hedge of thorns guarding seeds)
